doc.title: George "Pops" Foster and Mugsy Spanier Interview, 1957-04-21

title: Chicago in the twenties: Capone, tips and the Rex
summary: Mugsy on money, gangsters in the clubs, Friars Inn and the Valentine's Day massacre.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: When did you make those records with Mackenzie Condon? That was a little later, huh? Uh-huh. I just made one record with Eddie and the... It was one record then? Yeah. Be some changes made, found a new baby. That's the only one I made. I didn't make sugar and all that. You mean you just made two sides? That's it? That's all. Yeah. Then later when I went to New York or I made two, I made some. The Blue Busters. And what was life like for a musician in Chicago in the 20s? Very good then. Everything. If you couldn't make any money then it was your fault. That was the best deal. Money was just flowing like water because it was during commission days, you know. And all the big gangsters would come down, listen to music, and they all liked jazz. I worked at a place called the Rex, 22nd Estate. It used to open at one o'clock in the morning. That's when I was playing, I was through school and all that. I'd get through one job and then go to the Rex and work there every night. From one to six, seven o'clock in the morning. We got twenty, twenty-five dollars a week. And we'd make around $250 a week tips. Is that something? Oh, sure. Who used to come in there? Oh, Capone and all the gangsters used to come in there. Was there ever any trouble? Was I ever in trouble? No. Was there ever any trouble? No. No trouble at all. Remember they went out there. It was a good time. Perfect gentleman. You had good times, didn't you? Is that so? First thing Capone is due, you come in a place where you give the band a couple hundred dollars. It all depends on how you feel. All you want to drink. They were all that late. Remember they'd come down to Friars Inn. I'd get on a list of New Orleans Rhythm Kings. They'd do the same thing down there. Those guys, they really used to make some money in tips. Gee. They had a great big steel case with a big lock on it. And then between the entertainers and the band, oh they'd split maybe three, four hundred dollars a piece a week. Is that something? Oh shit. And every time one of those entertainers would go around the tables, sing a song. If he didn't come back with two, three hundred dollars or something else. Then we got smart in the cellar. We'd go around the tables with him because we'd find out about him first and we didn't know him so well. We'd go around and make sure, just watch and see what they get. And I'd come back and tell the fellas. They don't put it all in there and tell them about it. If Mike Fritzel found that out, he'd fire them. So they had to be honest. When Kapoor came, did he come with girls or were they just a bunch of men usually? Oh yeah, there's entourage, you know, guarding all around them. There'd be girls. Because they all like girls. I imagine they made a lot of money too. Who was that guy that Kapoor killed on Valentine's Day? Whose gang was that? With Moran? That was Doug's Moran. Boy, they could never prove him. When he killed his six. The Valentine's Day Massacre. Yeah. The Kilo Sixth guy? Yeah. That was in Clark State, in the 20 hundreds, in the back of the garage. Did you ever see him? Who, Kapoor? Moran. Oh yeah. He used to come down to Fryer's Inn. They all used to come. Every place, it'd work widely, you'd see some of them there all the time. Different nights. What was Fryer's Inn? That was at Van Buren and Wabash, downstairs in the basement. Was it a big place? Oh yes. That's where the New Orleans Rhythm King got to start.
